extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, patent policymakers, USPTO officials, and stakeholders in patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: A policy/advocacy brief arguing that the AIA's temporary Covered Business Method (CBM) review program should expire as scheduled, giving reasons why extension or expansion would be harmful or unnecessary. It evaluates the program's purpose, usage statistics, overlap with other post-grant proceedings, and effects on innovation and international obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary/transitional nature and sunset as scheduled
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 of the AIA created a temporary 'transitional' CBM review program—an eight-year program beginning in 2012 and scheduled to expire on September 16, 2020. Congress should reject efforts to extend or expand the program beyond its specific time and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The past eight years have provided more than enough time for petitioners to challenge covered business method patents; the USPTO has recommended 'adhering to the sunset period and discontinuing CBM proceedings on Sept. 16, 2020.' Any extension would undermine patent rights and drain USPTO resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program was intended for a narrow class of patents and users
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacted the CBM program as a temporary review process to respond to a very narrow class of financial services-related patents perceived to be improperly issued, and made it available only to persons sued for or charged with infringement of a business method patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program's original purpose and limited scope (financial-services-related business methods; parties sued/charged) is a basis for arguing against broadened or extended application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of IPR and PGR makes CBM unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA also created Inter Partes Review (IPR) and Post-Grant Review (PGR) proceedings, which have no sunset date and can be brought by any entity against any class of patents, including business method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because IPR and PGR can address the same concerns without a sunset, CBM is redundant; policymakers should consider overlap when evaluating whether to continue CBM.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM singles out an entire class of technology (discriminatory and unprecedented)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CBM review program is an unusual and unprecedented measure singling out an entire class of technology innovation for additional scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating business-method patents differently departs from the uniform incentives historically provided by the U.S. patent system and risks creating unequal treatment among invention types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague definition of 'covered business method patent' chills innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The vague definition of 'covered business method patent' in the AIA and USPTO regulations has already had a chilling effect on innovation in a number of industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief cites reports of decreased R&D in the software industry and warns that other areas (artificial intelligence, cybersecurity protocols, certain cancer therapies) could reduce innovation rates due to the threat of CBM review.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM stays in court proceedings allow infringers to delay enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the AIA permits courts to stay proceedings during the pendency of a CBM proceeding, alleged patent infringers can delay patent owners from enforcing their patent rights in court while the petitioner continues to infringe and gain market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural consequence is presented as a harm to patent owners and market incentives, and as a practical reason not to extend CBM.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM may violate international obligations and harm relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The process's discriminatory treatment and misapplication to other patents may violate the United States' obligations under the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) and encourage retaliation from trading partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should weigh potential WTO/TRIPS compliance risks and diplomatic/retaliatory consequences when considering extending or expanding CBM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declining usage statistics justify sunsetting the program
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB statistics show the number of CBM petitions filed has declined sharply—from 177 petitions filed in FY2014 to 22 in FY2019, and only 11 in the current year—indicating the program is now rarely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief uses these statistics to argue the program has served its transitional purpose and no longer warrants continuation; declining filings are cited as empirical support for sunset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension would undermine patent rights and drain USPTO resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Any further extension of the CBM program would undermine patent rights and drain resources from the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an overall policy criterion used to evaluate whether continuation is worth its cost: weigh harms to patent rights and administrative burden against any remaining benefits of CBM.
